rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He reads “before and behind” temporally: messengers came before Hud and Salih and after them.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: أي قبلهم وبعدهم، أي قبل هود وصالح وبعدهما

rows.speaker: الضحاك والفراء
rows.claim: The messengers before them were sent to their forefathers, while those behind them were present with them; the second pronoun refers to messengers.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من أرسل إلى آبائهم ومن أرسل إليهم فيكون من بين أيديهم معناه: من قبلهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Earlier messengers' warnings reached the lifetimes of Aad and Thamud, and later messengers came after their existence; together these establish the proof by report and direct encounter.
rows.anchor: ومن خلفهم: أي جاءهم رسول بعد تقدم وجودهم في الزمن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: The phrase means the messengers approached from every side and exhausted every means, like Satan's threat to approach people from all directions.
rows.anchor: أي آتوهم من كل جانب، واجتهدوا بهم وأعملوا فيهم كل حيلة

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: The messengers warned them with past nations' destruction and the future punishment of the afterlife.
rows.anchor: أنذروهم من وقائع الله فيمن قبلهم من الأمم وعذاب الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabari's split antecedents for the two pronouns depart from the apparent wording and produce an obscure, strained sense.
rows.anchor:
وفيه
خروج عن الظاهر في تفريق الضمائر وتعمية المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aad and Thamud are singled out because Quraysh knew their fate and encountered their lands in Yemen and al-Hijr.
rows.anchor: وخص بالذكر من الأمم المهلكة عاد وثمود لعلم قريش بحالهما

rows.speaker: الأفوه الأودي
rows.claim: His cited poem evokes the destruction of Aad and Thamud as evidence familiar to the audience.
rows.anchor: أضحوا كقيل بن عنز في عشيرته ... إذ أهلكت بالذي سدى لها عاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That they worship none but God” can be parsed with explanatory أن because the messengers' arrival entails speech, or as a lightened emphatic particle, or as a subjunctive linked to prohibitive لا.
rows.anchor: يصح أن تكون أن تفسيرية، لأن مجيء الرسل إليهم يتضمن معنى القول

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: He gives only the distant analysis in which لا is negative and أن governs the subjunctive.
rows.anchor: ويجوز على بعد أن تكون لا نافية، وأن ناصبة للفعل

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He supplies the omitted object of “if our Lord had willed” as sending angels.
rows.anchor: وقدره الزمخشري: لو شاء ربنا إرسال الرسل لأنزل ملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted object in this construction belongs to the answer's own category; the fuller sense is that God would have sent angels with the message if He willed.
rows.anchor:
لا يكون تقدير المحذوف ما قاله الزمخشري، وإنما التقدير:
لو شاء ربنا إنزال ملائكة بالرسالة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: That counterfactual makes their demand for angel messengers an even stronger denial of human messengers, since God did not will the former.
rows.anchor: وهذا أبلغ في الامتناع من إرسال البشر، إذ علقوا ذلك بأقوال الملائكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In “we disbelieve in what you were sent with,” ما may be a verbal noun or relative pronoun, with its pronoun returning to it; either way denial reaches the sending itself.
rows.anchor: وما مصدرية، أي بإرسالكم، وبه توكيد لذلك. ويجوز أن يكون ما بمعنى الذي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers' wording is taunting, not an admission that the messengers were truly sent; it means “what you claim to have been sent with.”
rows.anchor: وليس قوله: بما أرسلتم إقرارا بالإرسال، بل هو على سبيل التهكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The taunt parallels Pharaoh calling Moses' mission the alleged sending of the messengers.
rows.anchor: كما قال فرعون: إن رسولكم الذي أرسل إليكم لمجنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aad arrogantly refused the messengers' command without right, then voiced the pride in their hearts by claiming no one was stronger than they.
rows.anchor: أي تعاظموا عن امتثال أمر الله وعن ما جاءتهم به الرسل، بغير الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their boast came from their great bodies and force; God answered that the One who gave them this strength is stronger.
rows.anchor: وذلك لما أعطاهم الله من عظم الخلق وشدة البطش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although they knew God's signs, they denied them like a deposit-holder knowingly repudiating a claimant's property.
rows.anchor: مع علمهم بآيات الله، كانوا يجحدونها ولا يعترفون بها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb كان often signals continued or habitual action, and “strength” here stands for power; divine and human power share a general category while differing in their proper qualities.
rows.anchor: ولفظة كان في كثير من الاستعمال تشعر بالمداومة، وعبر بالقوة عن القدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God ordered the wind-keepers to release wind only through a ring-sized opening; a bull's-nostril opening would have destroyed the world.
rows.anchor: أنه تعالى أمر خزنة الريح ففتحوا عليهم قدر حلقة الخاتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another report says the wind carried camels with their loads and threw them into the sea.
rows.anchor: وروي أنها كانت تحمل العير بأوقادها، فترميهم في البحر

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He glosses ṣarṣar as intensely hot and scorching.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد: شديدة السموم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس والضحاك وقتادة والسدي
rows.claim: They derive ṣarṣar from cold, using the root ṣarr for chill.
rows.anchor:
وقال ابن عباس، والضحاك، وقتادة، والسدي:
من الصر، أي باردة

rows.speaker: السدي وأبو عبيدة وابن قتيبة والطبري
rows.claim: They connect ṣarṣar with a wind that makes a sound.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي أيضا، وأبو عبيدة، وابن قتيبة، والطبري، وجماعة: من صرصر إذا صوت

rows.speaker: ابن السكيت
rows.claim: He allows ṣarṣar to derive from ṣurra, a cry, and notes that Ṣarṣar is also an Iraqi river.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن السكيت: صرصر، يجوز أن يكون من الصرة، وهي الصيحة

rows.speaker: الحرميان وأبو عمرو والنخعي وعيسى والأعرج
rows.claim: They read naḥisāt with a still ḥāʾ, which may be a verbal noun used adjectivally or a shortened form.
rows.anchor:
وقرأ الحرميان،
وأبو عمرو، والنخعي، وعيسى، والأعرج نحسات، بسكون الحاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He questions the proposed adjectival pattern with a still middle radical, since the grammarians list no such adjective from an intransitive verb.
rows.anchor: وتتبعت ما ذكره التصريفيون مما جاء صفة من فعل اللازم فلم يذكروا فيه فعلا بسكون العين

rows.speaker: قتادة وأبو رجاء والجحدري وشيبة وأبو جعفر والأعمش وباقي السبعة
rows.claim: They read naḥisāt with kasra, which the author calls the regular form from naḥisa.
rows.anchor: وقرأ قتادة، وأبو رجاء، والجحدري، وشيبة، وأبو جعفر، والأعمش، وباقي السبعة: بكسر الحاء

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: He glosses naḥs and naḥis as “ill-starred” or accursed.
rows.anchor:
وقال الطبري:
نحس ونحس: مقت

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He analyzes the reading as a shortened form of naḥis, an adjective on faʿil, or an adjective derived from a verbal noun.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: مخفف نحس، أو صفة على فعل، أو وصف بمصدر

rows.speaker: مجاهد وقتادة والسدي
rows.claim: They explain the days as ill-omened in the familiar sense of misfortune.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد، وقتادة، والسدي: مشائيم من النحس المعروف

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He says the days were intensely cold, so that cold itself became their punishment.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: شديدة البرد، وحتى كان البرد عذابا لهم

rows.speaker: الأصمعي
rows.claim: He cites a line using naḥs for cold, as evidence for the lexical sense.
rows.anchor: وأنشد الأصمعي في النحس بمعنى البرد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation derives the days' description from dust, with a rajaz line glossing a low-dust day.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سميت بذلك لأنها ذات غبار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس ومجاهد وقتادة
rows.claim: They say the days came successively, from one Wednesday to the next at the end of Shawwal.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس، ومجاهد، وقتادة: متتابعات كانت آخر شوال من أربعاء إلى أربعاء

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He dates the first day to Sunday morning.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: أولها غداة يوم الأحد

rows.speaker: الربيع بن أنس
rows.claim: He identifies it as Friday.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع بن أنس: يوم الجمعة

rows.speaker: يحيى بن سلام
rows.claim: He identifies it as Sunday.
rows.anchor: وقال يحيى بن سلام: يوم الأحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The humiliating punishment means their destruction; the alternate reading with tāʾ makes the wind or the ill-omened days the subject of “make them taste.”
rows.anchor:
لنذيقهم عذاب الخزي في الحياة الدنيا:
وهو الهلاك. وقرىء: لتذيقهم بالتاء

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He treats the genitive as an attribute attached to the described punishment and says calling the punishment itself disgrace is more forceful than calling its victims disgraced.
rows.anchor: وأضاف العذاب إلى الخزي إضافة الموصوف إلى صفته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The narrative begins with Aad because they were earlier in time, then turns to Thamud.
rows.anchor: وبدأ بقصة عاد، لأنها أقدم زمانا، ثم ذكر ثمود

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة والسدي وابن زيد
rows.claim: They gloss “We guided them” as “We made the way clear to them.”
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس، وقتادة، والسدي، وابن زيد: بينا لهم

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says guidance here does not mean guidance that brings a person into guidance.
rows.anchor:
قال ابن عطية:
وليس الهدى هنا بمعنى الإرشاد

rows.speaker: الفراء والزمخشري
rows.claim: They interpret the guidance as making both the path of error and the path of right accessible, like the two paths in the cited verse.
rows.anchor: وقال الفراء، وتبعه الزمخشري: فهديناهم: فذللناهم على طريق الضلالة والرشد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He explains this usage as enabling them and removing every excuse, as though the means that entail guidance had produced its result; he calls the rival account Muʿtazilite.
rows.anchor: للدلالة على أنه مكنهم وأزاح عللهم ولم يبق لهم عذر ولا علة

rows.speaker: سفيان
rows.claim: He interprets the guidance as “We called them.”
rows.anchor: وقال سفيان: دعوناهم

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: He also glosses it as showing them the distinction between guidance and error.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن زيد: أعلمناهم الهدى من الضلال

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says choosing blindness describes their own acquired action, while creation of it belongs to God; the verse attributes it to their acquisition.
rows.anchor: فاستحبوا عبارة عن تكسبهم في العمى، وإلا فهو بالاختراع لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-hawn means humiliation; Ibn Miqsam's alternate reading gives ʿadhāb al-hawān.
rows.anchor: والهون: الهوان، وصف العذاب بالمصدر أو أبدل منه

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He calls the verse sufficient proof against the Qadariyya, whom he polemically labels this community's Magians.
rows.anchor: ولو لم يكن في القرآن حجة على القدرية الذين هم مجوس هذه الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He characterizes al-Zamakhshari's attack on Sunnis as his habitual polemic.
rows.anchor: على عادته في سب أهل السنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says 110 believers survived after responding to Hud and Salih.
rows.anchor: قيل: وكان من نجا من المؤمنين ممن استجاب هود وصالح مائة وعشرة أنفس

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative “the day” is governed by an understood “remember.”
rows.anchor: وانتصب يوم باذكر

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: They read “are gathered” in the passive, with “enemies of God” nominative.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: يحشر مبنيا للمفعول، وأعداء رفعا

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي ونافع والأعرج وأهل المدينة
rows.claim: They read in the first-person plural with “enemies” accusative; al-Aʿraj also has kasra on the shīn.
rows.anchor: وزيد بن علي، ونافع، والأعرج، وأهل المدينة: بالنون أعداء نصبا، وكسر الشين الأعرج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Until” marks the endpoint of the gathering, and God's enemies means all disbelievers, past and future.
rows.anchor: وحتى: غاية ليحشروا، أعداء الله: هم الكفار من الأولين والآخرين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says ما after “when” emphasizes that the time they reach Hell must be the time of their testimony.
rows.anchor: ومعنى التأكيد فيها أن وقت مجيئهم النار لا محالة أن يكون وقت الشهادة عليهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He sees no need for that emphasis: the conditional time construction already guarantees that testimony occurs then; the narrative implies they first deny their crimes.
rows.anchor: ولا أدري أن معنى زيادة ما بعد إذ التوكيد فيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted step is that they are questioned about their crimes and deny them, whereupon their senses testify to what they acquired.
rows.anchor: وفي الكلام حذف، التقدير: حتى إذا ما جاؤها، أي النار، وسئلوا عما أجرموا فأنكروا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the first human feature to speak is the left thigh, after which the limbs say that the person was defending himself through them.
rows.anchor: أن أول ما ينطق من الإنسان فخذه اليسرى، ثم تنطق الجوارح فيقول: تبا لك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Of the five senses, only hearing, sight, and touch are named because these involve moral duties; taste is part of touch, while smell carries no duty and is weak.
rows.anchor: اقتصر من الحواس على السمع والبصر واللمس، إذ هذه هي التي جاء فيها التكليف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of skins is literal; alternative explanations take them as a euphemism for limbs generally or for sexual organs.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الجلود هي المعروفة. وقيل: هي الجوارح كنى بها عنها

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He is among the majority of commentators who take “skins” as a euphemism for the sexual organs, as in “secret” for intercourse.
rows.anchor: وعليه أكثر المفسرين، منهم ابن عباس، كما كنى عن النكاح بالسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bodies testify to the crimes they committed, and when asked why, they give no cause beyond God's making them speak.
rows.anchor: بما كانوا يعملون من الجرائم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The guilty address their skins as rational witnesses because the skins have just given testimony.
rows.anchor: ولما صدر منها ما صدر من العقلاء، وهي الشهادة، خاطبوها بقولهم

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: He reads the question with a feminine plural pronoun, “why did you (fem.) testify?”
rows.anchor: وقرأ زيد بن علي: لم شهدتن؟ بضمير المؤنثات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Everything” need not be universal; it can mean whatever normally speaks or whatever is made to speak miraculously.
rows.anchor: لا يراد به العموم، بل المعنى: كل ناطق بما ذلك له عادة، أو كان ذلك فيه خرق عادة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He limits “everything” to animals, or to all things within divine power in another verse, and says God creates speech in the organs as He did in a tree.
rows.anchor:
أراد بكل شيء: كل شيء من الحيوان، كما أراد به في قوله:
والله على كل شيء قدير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He accuses al-Zamakhshari of importing Muʿtazilite theology: his tree analogy implies that the tree, rather than God, spoke to Moses.
rows.anchor: وهذا الرجل مولع بمذهبه الاعتزالي، يدخله في كل ما يقدر أنه يدخل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “You did not conceal yourselves” may be the limbs' speech, God's reproach, or an angel's speech.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قوله: وما كنتم تستترون من كلام الجوارح، قيل: ويحتمل أن يكون من كلام الله تعالى

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He construes the phrase as hiding out of fear that the limbs would testify, while the people did not know they could testify and thought God unaware of hidden deeds.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا نحا مجاهد، والستر يأتي في هذا المعنى

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He understands it as inability to hide their acts from their own limbs, whatever their disbelief or sin.
rows.anchor: وإلى هذا نحا السدي، أو ما كنتم تتوقعون بالاختفاء والستر أن يشهد عليكم

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He paraphrases “you did not conceal” as “you did not think,” a semantic gloss rather than a lexical synonym.
rows.anchor: وعبر قتادة عن تستترون بتظنون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their assumption that God did not know many of their deeds concerns hidden acts and is unbelief, ignorance, and a corrupt belief that entails doubting revelation and divine knowledge.
rows.anchor: ولكن ظننتم أن الله لا يعلم كثيرا، وهو الخفيات من أعمالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” points to their prior assumption, which is the subject; “destroyed you” is its predicate, and the following “your thought” is an apposition.
rows.anchor: وذلكم: إشارة إلى ظنهم أن الله لا يعلم كثيرا من أعمالهم، وهو مبتدأ خبره أرداكم، وظنكم بدل من ذلكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He analyzes both “your thought” and “destroyed you” as predicates.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: وظنكم وأرداكم خبران

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He allows “destroyed you” to be a second predicate.
rows.anchor:
وقال ابن عطية:
أرداكم يصلح أن يكون خبرا بعد خبر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects making “your thought” a predicate because it merely repeats what the demonstrative already identifies, producing a tautology.
rows.anchor: ولا يصح أن يكون ظنكم بربكم خبرا، لأن قوله: وذلكم إشارة إلى ظنهم السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Kufans allow the past verb as a circumstantial clause; Basrans generally require qad, though al-Akhfash correctly accepts an unmarked past circumstantial on abundant Arabic evidence.
rows.anchor: وقد أجاز الأخفش من البصريين وقوع الماضي حالا بغير تقدير قد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If they are patient” addresses the Prophet; an ellipsis may add “or are not patient,” or describe their persistence in abandoning the Prophet's religion and following desire.
rows.anchor: فإن يصبروا: خطاب للنبي عليه السلام، قيل: وفي الكلام حذف تقديره: أولا يصبروا

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He reads the active form as their asking pardon, but they will not be pardoned.
rows.anchor: قال الضحاك: إن يعتذروا فما هم من المعذورين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading takes the verb passively: they are asked to satisfy their Lord, but cannot act now that the abode of deeds has ended.
rows.anchor: أي طلب منهم أن يرضوا ربهم، فما هم فاعلون، ولا يكون ذلك لأنهم قد فارقوا الدنيا دار الأعمال

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A Prophetic report says there is no opportunity to seek redress after death.
rows.anchor:
كما
قال صلى الله عليه وسلم: «ليس بعد الموت مستعتب

rows.speaker: أبو ذؤيب
rows.claim: He cites a poem saying fate cannot be placated by those who grieve.
rows.anchor: والدهر ليس بمعتب من يجزع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God caused or assigned bad companions to them; قرناء means evil companions from the corrupt among jinn and humankind.
rows.anchor: أي سببنا لهم من حيث لم يحتسبوا. وقيل: سلطنا ووكلنا عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says their companions adorned denial of the afterlife, with no paradise, hell, or resurrection before them, and worldly error and pleasures behind them.
rows.anchor: من أمر الآخرة، أنه لا جنة ولا نار ولا بعث

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He interprets what lies before them as visible actions and what lies behind them as future actions.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: ما بين أيديهم: أعمالهم التي يشاهدونها، وما خلفهم: ما هم عاملوه في المستقبل

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He takes the phrase as their evil beliefs about messengers, worship of idols, and imitation of forefathers, followed by their rejection of resurrection.
rows.anchor: من معتقدات السوء في الرسل والنبوات ومدح عبادة الأصنام

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He sums up what lies before them as worldly affairs and what lies behind them as afterlife affairs.
rows.anchor: ما بين أيديهم من أمر الدنيا، وما خلفهم من أمر الآخرة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains God's assigning devils as abandonment of those resolutely committed to unbelief, leaving them with no companions but devils; he adduces the verse about a devil being assigned to one who turns away.
rows.anchor: معناه أنه خذلهم ومنعهم التوفيق لتصميمهم على الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He labels that explanation Muʿtazilite.
rows.anchor: وهو على طريقة الاعتزال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “In nations” means among a group or number of earlier nations; its syntactic position is circumstantial, and the pronoun “they” includes both the referents and those nations.
rows.anchor: في أمم: أي في جملة أمم، وعلى هذا قول الشاعر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's “they were losers” explains why punishment was deserved.
rows.anchor:
إنهم كانوا خاسرين:
الضمير لهم وللأمم، وهذا تعليل لاستحقاقهم العذاب

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: He explains “make noise in it” as entering into the Qur'an by attacking and criticizing it.
rows.anchor: قال أبو العالية: وقعوا فيه وعيبوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account says Quraysh deliberately whistled, clapped, shouted, and recited verse to drown out Muhammad when listeners gathered for his recitation.
rows.anchor: فخشي الكفار استمالة القلوب بذلك فقالوا: متى قرأ محمد صلى الله عليه وسلم، فلنلغط نحن بالمكاء والصفير

rows.speaker: الجمهور والفراء
rows.claim: They read the verb with fatḥa on the ghayn, deriving it from laghiya.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور والفراء: بفتح الغين مضارع لغي بكسرها

rows.speaker: ابن بكر السهمي وقتادة وأبو حيوة والزعفراني وابن أبي إسحاق وعيسى
rows.claim: They read with ḍamma on the ghayn, from laghā; the dialect means to insert useless talk into the recitation.
rows.anchor:
بضم الغين مضارع لغى بفتحها، وهما لغتان، أي ادخلوا فيه
اللغو

rows.speaker: الأخفش
rows.claim: He gives a dialect and phonological account of the two forms, noting the open vowel where a guttural makes it natural.
rows.anchor: وقال الأخفش: يقال لغا يلغى بفتح الغين وقياسه الضم، لكنه فتح لأجل حرف الحلق

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: He allows the fatḥa reading to mean “throw it away,” with fīhi understood as bihi.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يكون الفتح من لغى بالشيء يلغى به إذا رمى به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their aim in drowning the recitation was to prevail by erasing its influence and reputation.
rows.anchor: لعلكم تغلبون: أي تطمسون أمره وتميتون ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The promise of severe punishment threatens Quraysh both with worldly defeat, including Badr, and with the worst punishment in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: والعذاب الشديد في الدنيا كوقعة بدر وغيرها، والأسوأ يوم القيامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “That” refers to their afterlife recompense; “the Fire” can be apposition or the predicate of an omitted subject.
rows.anchor: ذلك: أي جزاؤهم في الآخرة، فالنار بدل أو خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling the Fire their “abode of eternity” makes the place its own container rhetorically, because its relation to them becomes its resting place.
rows.anchor: والمعنى أنها دار الخلد، كما قال تعالى: لقد كان لكم في رسول الله أسوة حسنة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says the Fire recompenses their distracting noise, while the text names the underlying cause, their denial of the signs.
rows.anchor: إن جزاءهم بما كانوا يلغون فيها، فذكر الجحود الذي هو سبب اللغو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Those who led us astray” can refer generally to each misleading jinn or human companion.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الذين يراد بهما الجنس، أي كل مغو من هذين النوعين

rows.speaker: علي وقتادة
rows.claim: They identify the two leaders as Iblis, who instituted unbelief, and Cain, who instituted unjust murder.
rows.anchor: وعن علي وقتادة: أنهما إبليس وقابيل، إبليس سن الكفر، وقابيل سن القتل بغير حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He objects that Cain was a sinful believer, whereas the damned seek those who led them into unbelief and eternal punishment; the proposed repair still clashes with the verse's wording.
rows.anchor: عن علي: وقابيل مؤمن عاص، وإنما طلبوا المضلين بالكفر المؤدي إلى الخلود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The request is to place the leaders in the lowest layer of Hell, the most severe torment, identified here with the hypocrites' level.
rows.anchor: يريدون في أسفل طبقة من النار، وهي أشد عذابا، وهي درك المنافقين

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Citing al-Khalil, he distinguishes arinī with kasra as “show me” from arinī with sukūn as a request to give the garment.
rows.anchor: حكوا عن الخليل أنك إذا قلت: أرني ثوبك بالكسر، فالمعنى: بصرنيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Basran grammarians disallow doubling the nūn of dual pronouns when spelled with yāʾ, but the canonical reading is evidence against them.
rows.anchor: وتشديد النون في اللذين واللتين وهذين وهاتين حالة كونهما بالياء لا تجيزه البصريون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage identifies the Sunna recitation with doubled nūn in these dual forms, challenging a grammatical rule.
rows.anchor: والقراءة بذلك في السبعة حجة عليهم

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says the verse was revealed about Abu Bakr: polytheists and Jews professed God but added false beliefs and did not remain upright, whereas Abu Bakr affirmed God alone and Muhammad as His servant and messenger.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عباس: نزلت في الصديق، قال المشركون: ربنا الله، والملائكة بناته، وهؤلاء شفعاؤنا عنده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the warning to unbelievers comes a warning to believers: professing God's lordship alone is not enough without matching belief; lordship knowledge precedes righteous action and steadfastness.
rows.anchor: وليس المراد التلفظ بالقول فقط، بل لا بد من الاعتقاد المطابق للقول اللساني

rows.speaker: سفيان بن عبد الله الثقفي
rows.claim: He asked the Prophet for a firming command; the Prophet said to affirm God as Lord and remain steadfast, then pointed to his tongue as what he most feared for him.
rows.anchor: قلت للنبي، صلى الله عليه وسلم: أخبرني بأمر أعتصم به، قال: «قل ربي الله ثم استقم

rows.speaker: الصديق
rows.claim: Abu Bakr explains steadfastness as remaining firm in monotheism without wavering in faith.
rows.anchor: وعن الصديق: ثم استقاموا على التوحيد، لم يضطرب إيمانهم

rows.speaker: عمر
rows.claim: Umar defines it as obeying God without fox-like maneuvering.
rows.anchor: وعن عمر: استقاموا لله بطاعته لم يروغوا روغان الثعالب

rows.speaker: عثمان
rows.claim: Uthman defines it as making one's deeds sincere.
rows.anchor: وعن عثمان: أخلصوا العمل

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: Ali defines it as performing the obligatory duties.
rows.anchor: وعن علي: أدوا الفرائض

rows.speaker: أبو العالية والسدي
rows.claim: They define steadfastness as sincerity and righteous action maintained until death.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية، والسدي: استقاموا على الإخلاص والعمل إلى الموت

rows.speaker: الثوري
rows.claim: He says they acted in accordance with what they professed.
rows.anchor: وقال الثوري: عملوا على وفاق ما قالوا

rows.speaker: الفضل
rows.claim: He defines steadfastness as renouncing the transient world and desiring the enduring one.
rows.anchor: وقال الفضل: زهدوا في الفانية ورغبوا في الباقية

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: He says they turned away from everything besides God.
rows.anchor: وقال الربيع: أعرضوا عن ما سوى الله تعالى

rows.speaker: الحسن وقتادة وجماعة
rows.claim: They define steadfastness by obedience and avoidance of sins.
rows.anchor: وعن الحسن وقتادة وجماعة: استقاموا بالطاعات واجتناب المعاصي

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He says ثم signals a step in rank: steadfastness is more important than verbal confession, as in the verse about believers not doubting.
rows.anchor:
وثم لتراخي الاستقامة عن الإقرار في
المرتبة وفضلها عليه

rows.speaker: الصديق
rows.claim: After asking what steadfastness meant, Abu Bakr rejects the answer “they did not sin” as too demanding and says it means they did not return to idol worship.
rows.anchor: حملتم الأمر على أشده، قالوا: فما تقول؟ قال لم يرجعوا إلى عبادة الأوثان

rows.speaker: مجاهد والسدي
rows.claim: They say the angels descend at death; Muqatil says at resurrection, and another view includes death, the grave, and resurrection.
rows.anchor: قال مجاهد والسدي: عند الموت. وقال مقاتل: عند البعث

rows.speaker: الحوفي وأبو البقاء
rows.claim: They parse أن as a subjunctive particle introducing “that you do not fear or grieve.”
rows.anchor: وأن ناصبة للمضارع، أي بانتفاء خوفكم وحزنكم

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He takes أن as “that is to say” or as a lightened emphatic, with an understood pronoun and prohibitive لا.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: بمعنى أي أو المخففة من الثقيلة، وأصله بأنه لا تخافوا

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He interprets the reassurance as freedom from fear of what lies ahead and grief for worldly things left behind.
rows.anchor: لا تخافوا ما تقدرون عليه، ولا تحزنوا على ما خلفتم من دنياكم

rows.speaker: عطاء بن أبي رباح
rows.claim: He says the angels promise that the believers' reward is accepted and their sins forgiven.
rows.anchor: ألا تخافوا رد ثوابكم، فإنه مقبول ولا تحزنوا على ذنوبكم

rows.speaker: عبد الله
rows.claim: His reading omits أن so the angels directly say “do not fear or grieve.”
rows.anchor: وفي قراءة عبد الله: لا تخافوا، بإسقاط أن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “We are your allies” is apparently the angels speaking; in Abdullah's reading it is part of their earlier direct quotation and means they were guardians in worldly life and are allies in the next.
rows.anchor: الظاهر أنه من كلام الملائكة، أي يقولون لهم

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He explains the angels' claim as protecting the believers in worldly life and being their allies in the afterlife.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: نحن حفظتكم في الدنيا، وأولياؤكم في الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes “we are your allies” as God's speech, meaning support through sufficiency and guidance.
rows.anchor:
وقيل: نحن أولياؤكم
من كلام الله تعالى، أولياؤكم بالكفاية والهداية

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He takes “therein” as referring to the afterlife.
rows.anchor: الضمير عائد على الآخرة، قاله ابن عطية

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: He takes “therein” as referring to Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقال الحوفي: على الجنة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He glosses what the believers ask for as what they wish for.
rows.anchor: قال مقاتل: ما تتمنون

rows.speaker: ابن عيسى
rows.claim: He says everything a believer claims as his is granted through the Lord's judgment.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عيسى: ما تدعي أنه لك، فهو لك بحكم ربك

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He glosses the promise as everything believers request.
rows.anchor: قال ابن عطية: ما تطلبون

rows.speaker: ابن عطاء
rows.claim: He explains nuzulan as the provision first offered to a guest.
rows.anchor: الرزق المقدم للنزيل وهو الضيف، قال معناه ابن عطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nuzulan can be a circumstantial noun of hospitality; others treat it as a verbal noun or the plural of nāzil used as a circumstantial.
rows.anchor: فيكون نزلا حالا، أي تعطون ذلك في حال كونه نزولا لا نزلا

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: He glosses the word as “a lodging from Us”; another view says it means reward.
rows.anchor: وقال الحسن: معنى نزلا منا، وقيل: ثوابا

rows.speaker: أبو حيوة
rows.claim: He reads nuzulan with a still zāy.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو حيوة: نزلا بإسكان الزاي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best speech belongs to anyone who calls people to God's oneness, acts righteously, and submits to God; the verse's scope appears general.
rows.anchor: أي لا أحد أحسن قولا ممن يدعو إلى توحيد الله، ويعمل العمل الصالح

rows.speaker: الحسن ومقاتل وجماعة
rows.claim: They likewise take the verse generally as concerning everyone who calls to God.
rows.anchor: والظاهر العموم في كل داع إلى الله، وإلى العموم ذهب الحسن ومقاتل وجماعة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the caller specifically as the Messenger, who invited to Islam, acted well toward God, and made Islam his religion.
rows.anchor: فقال ابن عباس: هو رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، دعا إلى الإسلام

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: A second report from him identifies them as the Prophet's Companions.
rows.anchor: وعنه أيضا: هم أصحاب رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم

rows.speaker: عائشة وقيس بن أبي حازم وعكرمة ومجاهد
rows.claim: They say it was revealed about callers to prayer; the author treats callers as included rather than exclusive because the surah is Meccan and the call to prayer was instituted in Medina.
rows.anchor: وينبغي أن يتأول قولهم على أنهم داخلون في الآية، وإلا فالسورة بكمالها مكية بلا خلاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling to God includes inviting people to Islam, fighting unbelievers, and restraining oppressors.
rows.anchor: والدعاء إلى الله يكون بالدعاء إلى الإسلام وبجهاد الكفار وكف الظلمة

rows.speaker: زيد بن علي
rows.claim: He says one calls to God by the sword; the author links this to his armed action against some Umayyad rulers.
rows.anchor: وقال زيد بن علي: دعا إلى الله بالسيف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zayd was learned in the Qur'an and transmitted an extensive commentary while imprisoned by Hisham ibn Abd al-Malik; the author had seen a substantial portion of it.
rows.anchor: وكان زيد هذا عالما بكتاب الله، وقد وقفت على جملة من تفسيره كتاب الله

rows.speaker: أبو العالية
rows.claim: He explains righteous action as praying between the call to prayer and the call to begin prayer.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو العالية: وعمل صالحا: صلى بين الأذان والإقامة

rows.speaker: عكرمة
rows.claim: He defines it as prayer and fasting.
rows.anchor: وقال عكرمة: صلى وصام

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He defines it as fulfilling the obligatory duties.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: أدى الفرائض

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He says the verse requires joining monotheistic Muslim belief, good action, and calling others to good.
rows.anchor: هي عامة في كل من جمع بين هذه الثلاثة أن يكون موحدا معتقدا لدين الإسلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He notes that the preceding interpretation describes the Muʿtazila, who called themselves people of justice and monotheism, and cites Ibn Abi al-Hadid's poem affirming those principles.
rows.anchor: ويعني بذلك المعتزلة، يسمون أنفسهم أهل العدل والتوحيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “I am one of the Muslims” means that submission is his creed, not merely something he said.
rows.anchor: ليس المعنى أنه تكلم بهذا، بل جعل الإسلام معتقده

rows.speaker: ابن أبي عبلة وإبراهيم بن نوح
rows.claim: They read وقال إني rather than the majority's وقال إنني.
rows.anchor: وقرأ ابن أبي عبلة، وإبراهيم بن نوح عن قتيبة الميال: وقال إني

rows.speaker: أبو بكر بن العربي
rows.claim: He argues that the verse says “I am a Muslim” without adding “if God wills,” against those who qualify their profession of Islam in that way.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو بكر بن العربي: لم يشترط إلا إن شاء الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because a person who calls others to God may face hostility, he should convey good gently and tactfully.
rows.anchor: وأن الداعي إلى الله قد يجافيه المدعو، فينبغي أن يرفق به ويتلطف في إيصال الخير فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says the verse was revealed about Abu Sufyan, an enemy of the Messenger who became a close friend.
rows.anchor: قيل: ونزلت في أبي سفيان بن حرب، وكان عدوا لرسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم، فصار وليا مصافيا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the good as saying “There is no god but God” and the evil as associating partners with God.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: الحسنة لا إله إلا الله، والسيئة الشرك

rows.speaker: الكلبي
rows.claim: He takes the contrast to be the two rival invitations: to monotheism and to associationism.
rows.anchor: وقال الكلبي: الدعوتان إليهما

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: He explains good and evil as forbearance and obscenity.
rows.anchor: وقال الضحاك: الحلم والفحش

rows.speaker: علي
rows.claim: He identifies good and evil as love of the Messenger and his family versus hatred of them.
rows.anchor: وعن علي: حب الرسول وآله وبغضهم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other illustrative contrasts are patience versus aversion, leniency versus harshness, and pardon versus moderation; these examples are not exhaustive.
rows.anchor:
وقيل:
الصبر والنفور. وقيل: المداراة والغلظة. وقيل: العفو والاقتصاد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The order “repel with what is better” intensifies the command: whoever finds superior repayment easy will find merely good repayment easy too.
rows.anchor: ولما تفاوتت الحسنة والسيئة، أمر أن يدفع السيئة بالأحسن، وذلك مبالغة

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He says كأن marks a comparison because an actual enemy does not become an intimate ally, though he may seem one outwardly.
rows.anchor: لأن الذي عنده عداوة لا يعود وليا حميما، وإنما يحسن ظاهره

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He identifies the better response as patience when angry, forbearance when treated ignorantly, and forgiving injury.
rows.anchor: وعن ابن عباس: بالتي هي أحسن: الصبر عند الغضب، والحلم عند الجهل، والعفو عند الإساءة

rows.speaker: مجاهد وعطاء
rows.claim: They say the better response begins with greeting the opponent on meeting.
rows.anchor: وقال مجاهد، وعطاء: السلام عند اللقاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Greeting at a meeting is only the beginning of the superior response, not its full extent.
rows.anchor: أي هو مبدأ الدفع بالأحسن، لأنه محصور فيه

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He also recommends turning away from their harm.
rows.anchor: وعن مجاهد أيضا: أعرض عن أذاهم

rows.speaker: أبو فراس الحمداني
rows.claim: His poem commends continual patient forgiveness as the best response to injury.
rows.anchor: يجني علي وأجنو صافحا أبدا ... لا شيء أحسن من جان على جان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The feminine pronoun refers to the trait or disposition of repelling evil with a better response.
rows.anchor: وما يلقاها: الضمير عائد على الفعلة والسجية التي هي الدفع بالأحسن

rows.speaker: طلحة بن مصرف وابن كثير
rows.claim: They have an alternate reading with yāʾ, from the verb meaning to meet or encounter.
rows.anchor: وقرأ طلحة بن مصرف، وابن كثير في رواية: وما يلاقاها: من الملاقاة

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: They read the verb as receiving or being granted the trait.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: من التلقي

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He says only those steadfast in obedience and turning away from desires attain this rare virtue; it is praise for them.
rows.anchor: إلا لمن كان صابرا على الطاعات، صارفا عن الشهوات

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He reads the great fortune as the reward of the afterlife, making the verse a promise.
rows.anchor: ذو حظ عظيم من ثواب الآخرة، قاله قتادة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported readings of the great fortune are intelligence or good character.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إلا ذو عقل. وقيل: ذو خلق حسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The repeated “only those steadfast receive it” emphasizes the excellence of this noble trait.
rows.anchor: وكرر وما يلقاها تأكيدا لهذه الفعلة الجميلة الجليلة

rows.speaker: مكي
rows.claim: He says the pronoun means the testimony that there is no god but God; the author considers this far-fetched.
rows.anchor: وحكى مكي: وما يلقاها: أي شهادة أن لا إله إلا الله، وفيه بعد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because people may sometimes answer an injury with another injury, they are told to seek refuge in God when Satan prompts such retaliation; the author links this to al-Aʿraf's closing passage.
rows.anchor: فأمره، إن عرض له ذلك، أن يستعيذ بالله، فإن ذلك من نزغ الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After presenting calling to God as the best speech and action, the text adduces celestial and terrestrial signs as proof of God's power, wisdom, and case.
rows.anchor: أردفه بذكر الدلائل العلوية والسفلية، وعلى قدرته الباهرة وحكمته البالغة وحجته القاطعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night comes first because darkness is absence while light is existence; the sun follows the day because it illuminates the world more than the moon, whose light is said to derive from the sun.
rows.anchor: قيل تنبيها على أن الظلمة عدم والنور وجود، وناسب ذكر الشمس بعد النهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some people worshipped the sun, as in the account of the Queen of Sheba and her people.
rows.anchor: وكان ناس يعبدون الشمس، كما جاء في قصة بلقيس وقومها

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the feminine plural pronoun “them” as agreement with an unintelligent plural understood as feminine.
rows.anchor: لأن حكم جماعة ما لا يعقل حكم الأنثى، أي الإناث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says al-Zamakhshari's explanation should distinguish small plurals from large ones; the passage coordinates four entities rather than a single plural noun.
rows.anchor: وكان ينبغي أن يفرق بين جمع القلة من ذلك، فإن الأفصح أن يكون كضمير الواحدة

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He also says “them” returns to the implied plural āyāt in “among His signs.”
rows.anchor: ولما قال: ومن آياته، كن في معنى الآيات، فقيل: خلقهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations return the pronoun to the signs just mentioned, or to sun and moon, which can be treated as a plural because of their differing cycles.
rows.anchor: وقيل: يعود على الآيات المتقدم ذكرها. وقيل: على الشمس والقمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “If you truly worship Him” means that genuine worshippers affirm God's oneness and do not associate partners with Him.
rows.anchor: إن كنتم موحدين غير مشركين

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: He places the prostration at “you worship,” because the prostration word has appeared just before it; the author reports a supporting narration from Masruq and Ibn Masud.
rows.anchor: والسجدة عند الشافعي عند قوله: تعبدون، وهي رواية مسروق عن عبد الله

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وابن وهب والشافعي
rows.claim: They place the prostration at “they do not tire,” treating that clause as completing the meaning; reports also name several early Muslims who prostrated there.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن وهب والشافعي: عند يسأمون، وبه قال أبو حنيفة، وسجد عندها ابن عباس وابن عمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who proudly refuse to bow to created celestial bodies are answered by angels near God, who glorify Him without tiring despite their superior rank.
rows.anchor: فإن استكبروا: أي تعاظموا على اجتناب ما نهيت من السجود لهذين المحدثين المربوبين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing that calling to God and its proofs are the greatest acts, the passage returns to threaten those disputing God's signs.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أن الدعاء إلى دين الله أعظم القربات

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He glosses deviation from God's signs as denial.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: هنا الإلحاد: التكذيب

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: He interprets the deviation as whistling, clapping, and making noise.
rows.anchor: ومجاهد: المكاء والصفير واللغو

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He explains it as putting speech in the wrong place.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: وضع الكلام غير موضعه

rows.speaker: أبو مالك
rows.claim: He says it means turning away from God's signs.
rows.anchor: وقال أبو مالك: يميلون عن آياتنا

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He says it means stubbornly opposing the messengers over the proofs and signs they brought.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: يعاندون رسلنا فيما جاءوا فيه من البينات والآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question about entering Hell or arriving safe is a rhetorical forcing choice, though the two outcomes are not comparable; being cast into Hell intimates the destination of Paradise, and arrival in safety counters the unbeliever's fear.
rows.anchor: ولا اشتراك بين الإلقاء في النار والإتيان آمنا، لكنه، كما قلنا، استفهام تقرير

rows.speaker: ابن بحر
rows.claim: He says the contrast applies generally to every unbeliever and believer.
rows.anchor: وهذه الآية، قال ابن بحر: عامة في كل كافر ومؤمن

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He says the verse was revealed about Abu Jahl and Uthman ibn Affan.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: نزلت في أبي جهل وعثمان بن عفان

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported pairings are Abu Jahl with Ammar, Umar, Hamza, or the Messenger.
rows.anchor: وقيل: في أبي جهل وحمزة بن عبد المطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Do what you will” is a threatening imperative; the reminder that God sees their deeds promises recompense.
rows.anchor: وعيد وتهديد بصيغة الأمر، ولذا جاء إنه بما تعملون بصير فيجازيكم بأعمالكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The Reminder” means the Qur'an, by agreement, and “those who disbelieved” means Quraysh and other disbelievers.
rows.anchor: والذكر: القرآن هو بإجماع، وخبر إن اختلفوا فيه أمذكور هو أو محذوف

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو بن العلاء
rows.claim: When Bilal ibn Abi Burda could not parse the predicate of إن, Abu Amr said it was close at hand in “those are called from a distant place.”
rows.anchor: إنه منك لقريب أولئك ينادون

rows.speaker: الحوفي
rows.claim: He objects that this predicate is too far away and that the verse already identifies the people called from afar.
rows.anchor: ويرد على هذا القول كثرة الفصل، وأنه ذكر هناك من تكون الإشارة إليهم

rows.speaker: عيسى بن عمر
rows.claim: He asks Amr ibn Ubayd about the syntax; Amr supplies an understood “they denied it” before describing the Qur'an as a mighty book, and Isa approves.
rows.anchor: وسأل عيسى بن عمر عمرو بن عبيد عن ذلك فقال عمرو: معناه في التفسير

rows.speaker: قوم
rows.claim: Some estimate a deleted predicate such as “they are obstinate” or “they are doomed.”
rows.anchor: وقال قوم: تقديره معاندون أو هالكون

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: He says the earlier rhetorical question supplies the predicate's meaning, perhaps that they will remain in Hell.
rows.anchor: وقال الكسائي: قد سد مسده ما تقدم من الكلام قبل إن

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He treats the clause about those who disbelieve in the Qur'an as apposition to the clause about those who deviate from God's signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: فإن قلت: بم اتصل قوله: إن الذين كفروا بالذكر؟ قلت: هو بدل من قوله: إن الذين يلحدون في آياتنا

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: He prefers the predicate to appear after the Qur'an's description as a mighty book, since its description belongs with the Reminder.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عطية: والذي يحسن في هذا هو إضمار الخبر بعد حكيم حميد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says the predicate is present in “falsehood does not approach it”: their falsehood cannot overturn its truth; alternatively the predicate is the later statement that the Prophet hears what earlier messengers heard.
rows.anchor: والذي أذهب إليه أن الخبر مذكور، لكنه حذف منه عائد يعود على اسم إن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, “nothing is said to you except what was said to earlier messengers” is the predicate, describing the deniers' bad outcome as with earlier peoples.
rows.anchor:
أو يكون الخبر قوله:
ما يقال لك إلا ما قد قيل للرسل من قبلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause “it is a mighty book” can be circumstantial, describing the Qur'an even as its deniers reject it; its unmatched inimitability or dominance over prior scriptures explains its might.
rows.anchor: وإنه لكتاب عزيز: جملة حالية، كما تقول: جاء زيد وإن يده على رأسه

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He calls the Qur'an noble and dear to God.
rows.anchor:
وقال ابن عباس:
عزيز كريم على الله تعالى

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: He says the Qur'an is protected from Satan.
rows.anchor: وقال مقاتل: ممتنع من الشيطان

rows.speaker: السدي
rows.claim: He says the Qur'an is uncreated.
rows.anchor: وقال السدي: غير مخلوق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation is that sound meanings make the Qur'an immune to criticism and it is guarded by God.
rows.anchor: وقيل: وصف بالعزة لأنه لصحة معانيه ممتنع الطعن فيه والإزراء عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Falsehood cannot approach the Qur'an from any direction; this is a metaphor for there being no route for criticism to reach it.
rows.anchor: واللفظ لا يخص الشيطان

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He interprets falsehood as Satan, although the author says the wording is not limited to Satan.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة: الباطل الشيطان

rows.speaker: ابن جبير والضحاك
rows.claim: They interpret what is before the Qur'an as prior scripture invalidating it and what is behind it as later scripture superseding it; the text can use falsehood in the causative sense of one who invalidates.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير والضحاك: من بين يديه: أي كتاب من قبله فيبطله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other interpretations place the phrase before and after revelation, with some reversing which side means before or after.
rows.anchor: وقيل: من بين يديه: أي قبل أن يتم نزوله، ولا من خلفه: من بعد نزوله

rows.speaker: الطبري
rows.claim: He says no falsifier can change or distort the Qur'an from either direction.
rows.anchor: وقال الطبري: من بين يديه: لا يقدر ذو باطل أن يكيده بتغيير ولا تبديل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “A revelation” apposes the Qur'an; the wise is its ruler or one who makes its meanings firm, and the praiseworthy is praised for its benefits and other blessings.
rows.anchor: تنزيل: أي هو تنزيل، من حكيم: أي حاكم أو محكم لمعانيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If God is the speaker in “nothing is said to you,” the message may concern shared laws or the fate of earlier deniers; limiting revelation to the following statement alone is too narrow, so “your Lord” begins a separate warning and comfort.
rows.anchor: وهذا التأويل فيه بعد، لأنه حصر ما أوحى الله إليه وإلى الرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the unbelievers are speaking: their abusive words and attacks on revelation repeat what earlier messengers heard; the verse then promises forgiveness for the obedient and punishment for the disobedient.
rows.anchor: ويحتمل أن يكون القائل الكفار، أي ما يقول لك كفار قومك إلا ما قد قال كفار الرسل

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: He says the verse consoles the Prophet, just as earlier communities called their messengers sorcerers or madmen.
rows.anchor:
وقال قتادة: عزى الله نبيه وسلاه بقوله:
ما يقال لك إلا ما قد قيل للرسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the Qur'an had been in a foreign tongue, the opponents would still have objected that its verses should be made clear; their demand arises from obstinacy, not a search for truth.
rows.anchor: لم يتركوا الاعتراض، ولقالوا لولا فصلت آياته: أي بينت لنا

rows.speaker: الجمهور
rows.claim: They read آعجمي with one interrogative hamza followed by the lengthened hamza of أعجمي, normally eased between vowel qualities.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الجمهور: آعجمي بهمزة الاستفهام بعدها مدة هي همزة أعجمي

rows.speaker: الأخوان والأعمش وحفص
rows.claim: They read two hamzas as an incredulous question: a foreign Qur'an sent to an Arab messenger or recipient?
rows.anchor: وقرأ الأخوان، والأعمش، وحفص: بهمزتين، أي وقالوا منكرين: أقرآن أعجمي ورسول عربي

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: He interprets their objection as asking what use a foreign-language book would be to Arabs.
rows.anchor: وتأوله ابن جبير أن معنى قوله: أعجمي، ونحن عرب ما لنا وللعجمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects Ibn Atiyya's interpretation of a mixed Arabic-and-foreign Qur'an because the hypothetical request is for a wholly foreign Qur'an, not a mixture.
rows.anchor: ولم يقترحوا أن يكون القرآن أعجميا وعربيا

rows.speaker: ابن جبير
rows.claim: For the reading without interrogative hamza and with still ʿayn, he says they wanted separate passages, some foreign and some Arabic.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن جبير معناه: لولا فصل فصلين، فكان بعضه أعجميا يفهمه العجم

rows.speaker: صاحب اللوامح
rows.claim: He explains this reading as their repeating the objection with an understood predicate: the Qur'an is foreign while its messenger is Arab.
rows.anchor: وقال صاحب اللوامح: لأنهم لما قالوا: لولا فصلت آياته، أعادوا القول ثانيا

rows.speaker: عمرو بن ميمون
rows.claim: He reads an interrogative hamza with fatḥa on ʿayn: whatever form the Qur'an took, the opponents would have objected because they did not seek truth.
rows.anchor: وقرأ عمرو بن ميمون: أعجمي بهمزة استفهام وفتح العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aʿjamī denotes foreign origin, while aʿjamī with still ʿayn describes someone unable to speak clearly; the yāʾ can intensify the adjective, as in aḥmarī and duwārī.
rows.anchor: والعجمي المنسوب إلى العجم، والياء للنسب على الحقيقة وأما إذا سكنت العين فهو الذي لا يفصح

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He explains the Arab objection by analogy with seeing a foreign book addressed to Arabs and asking whether its book is foreign but its recipient Arab.
rows.anchor: هو على ما يجب أن يقع في إنكار المنكر لو رأى كتابا عجميا كتب إلى قوم من العرب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He approves the rhetorical point but says al-Zamakhshari needlessly multiplies words and embellishments.
rows.anchor: وهو حسن، إلا أن فيه تكثيرا على عادته في حب الشقشقة والتفهيق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For believers, the Qur'an guides to truth and heals doubt and suspicion in their hearts.
rows.anchor: هدى: أي إرشاد إلى الحق، وشفاء: أي لما في الصدور من الظن والشك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent syntax makes “those who do not believe” a subject and “in their ears is deafness” its predicate.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن والذين لا يؤمنون مبتدأ، وفي آذانهم وقر هو موضع الخبر

rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: He posits an omitted subject “it,” meaning the Qur'an is deafness in the unbelievers' ears and blindness over them.
rows.anchor: وقال الزمخشري: هو في آذانهم وقر على حذف المبتدأ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says the clause is complete without an implied هو; attaching it to the preceding preposition forces coordination across two governing words and a disputed construction.
rows.anchor: ولا يضطر إلى إضمار هو، فالكلام تام دونه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition على portrays blindness as prevailing over unbelievers, while ل for believers marks the Qur'an's particular benefit to them.
rows.anchor: وجاء بلفظ عليهم الدالة على استيلاء العمى عليهم، وجاء في حق المؤمنين باللام الدالة على الاختصاص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preceding promise of recompense prompts the question of when it occurs; only God knows the appointed Hour, and knowledge of hidden events belongs to Him.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى من عمل صالحا الآية، كان في ذلك دلالة على الجزاء يوم القيامة، وكأن سائلا قال: ومتى ذلك؟ فقيل: لا يعلمها إلا الله

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر والأعرج وشيبة وقتادة والحسن ونافع وابن عامر
rows.claim: These readers have “what emerges” in a form that takes fruits collectively, while al-Mufaḍḍal, Ḥafṣ, and Ibn Miqsam read “fruits” in the plural; the remaining canonical readers and other authorities use the singular.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر، والأعرج، وشيبة، وقتادة، والحسن بخلاف عنه ونافع، وابن عامر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fruit emerging from its sheath and pregnancy and birth create things after nonexistence, so they fit the discussion of God's knowledge of the Hour and prove resurrection as re-creation after annihilation.
rows.anchor: ولما كان ما يخرج من أكمام الشجرة وما تحمل الإناث وتضعه هو إيجاد أشياء بعد العدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question “where are My partners?” on Judgment Day is mockery and rebuke directed to all who worship anything besides God.
rows.anchor: والضمير في يناديهم عام في كل من عبد غير الله، فيندرج فيه عباد الأوثان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The called unbelievers say “we have informed You”; the author takes “we inform You” as a performative response, with the repeated question serving to rebuke them.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن قولهم: آذناك إنشاء، كقولك: أقسمت لأضربن زيدا

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: He glosses ādhannāka as “we have made You hear,” avoiding the implication of informing God, since those at the Resurrection know God already knows all things.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس: أسمعناك، كأنه استبعد الإعلام لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent speaker is the people addressed, who now deny seeing anyone who could testify that God has partners; another view makes the alleged partners themselves say they did not witness the association.
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن الضمير في قالوا عائد على المنادين، لأنهم المحدث معهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase “none of us is a witness today” is syntactically the object of ādhannāka, which here means informing.
rows.anchor: وآذناك معلق لأنه بمعنى الإعلام. والجملة من قوله: ما منا من شهيد في موضع المفعول
